predicted_signals.evidence: Residents leave shelter before all-clear
Residents enter shelter or follow instructions incompletely (late entry, partial compliance)
Residents refuse protective guidance because they distrust the source or alert system
Community members informally pressure others to follow safety protocols
Gatherings that violate safety guidelines
A defensive measure demonstrably averted harm (Iron Dome interception, mamad/shelter doctrine, drill saved lives in documented hit)
Documented close call where protective measures barely prevented harm
Residents take calculated risk to reduce another harm (e.g. driving during alert to relieve childcare burden)
Community actors resolve conflicts constructively, enabling cooperation (mediation, compromise, de-escalation)
Faith-based communal coping (prayer assemblies, tehillim groups, ritualized mourning)
Constructive cooperation across religious lines during the emergency
Conflict or tension specifically along religious lines
Residents actively ask neighbors or institutions for help (distinct from offering help)
Constructive cooperation across class, ethnic, or geographic lines (not only religious)
Cooperation across community lines breaks down or is blocked
Free-riding or norm-breaking in shared emergency resources (shelter hogging, aid queue jumping)
Residents or affected groups voice concrete loss of trust in named leadership (broken promises, false reassurances, perceived dishonesty about emergency conditions)
Residents or named civic figures publicly demand accountability or express distrust of the political/governmental handling of the emergency (specific policy demands, not general partisan opinion)
Community actors reach working consensus on goals/priorities and a plan for action (collaboration, agreement on what to do next)
Mistrust/conflict prevents working consensus or blocks collective action (dissensus, infighting, inability to agree on priorities)
Inter-agency or inter-organization coordination breaks down
Multiple agencies, services, or organizations coordinate effectively in response
Authorities visibly act on community input, complaints, or requests
Constructive civic participation (public hearings, lawful protest with concrete demands, organized petitioning)
NGOs or civil-society organizations step up with organized non-state response
Public requests for explanations that are answered or visibly addressed (distinct from unanswered political_distrust)
Non-official community figures step up with visible coordination or guidance
Named leaders deflect responsibility rather than address the emergency
Named leaders publicly accept responsibility and commit to corrective action
Leadership visibility without substantive delivery (photo-ops, empty gestures)
Central authority devolves decision-making to local actors effectively
Rumors or misinformation are circulating
Authorities, experts, or community members visibly correct circulating rumors or misinformation
Residents rely on or explicitly trust a specific local/official source for emergency information (trusted hotline, known local authority, trusted broadcaster)
Residents explicitly distrust or disregard an emergency information source (source seen as unreliable/lying/ignored), reducing adherence
A working channel exists for the public to ask questions / articulate needs and receive responses (hotline, municipal desk, two-way messaging)
Public feedback/inquiry channels are absent, unreachable, or ignored (hotline down, no response, no way to ask/clarify)

Residents actively seek out emergency or protective guidance — shelter locations, HFC instructions, evacuation routes, operational alerts. NOT: legal, financial, religious, or personal planning inform
Guidance is specific, situation-matched, and demonstrably leads to correct protective behavior
Guidance exists but fails to help — does not match real constraints, too vague to act on, or leaves critical scenarios uncovered
Emergency information adapted for at-risk groups (Arabic translations, accessible formats, elder outreach, special-needs channels)
Emergency information not reaching at-risk groups (no Arabic, inaccessible formats, elders/disabled left uninformed)
Identified foreign or coordinated disinformation push (state actors, bot networks) — distinct from organic rumor_spread
Residents intentionally tune out emergency news or alerts as coping
Ordinary residents (not authorities) visibly correct misinformation or verify claims
Residents overwhelmed by volume of alerts or conflicting streams (distinct from confusion about content)
Communication drops off after acute phase leaving residents uninformed
Emergency guidance uses register or language residents cannot understand or act on
Authorities tell residents when the next update will come or what is still unknown
No timeline or commitment for next information — residents left in uncertainty about future updates
Civilian daily routines (commuting, shopping, leisure, social rhythms) are visibly disrupted by the emergency — distinct from named-institution closures, which are service_disruption
Residents are evacuated, displaced, or unable to return home because of the emergency (named community, hotel/relative housing, prolonged absence)
Residents self-evacuated from Kiryat Shmona before the municipality issued orders
Evacuees return home or displacement is visibly resolved (mirror of evacuation_displacement)
A named system continues operating effectively despite documented elevated demand or disruption
Local economic activity (employment, business, commerce) sustains during the emergency
Local economic activity is disrupted: business closures, lost income, employment freeze due to the emergency
Communities visibly recover after a hit: re-opening, return of evacuees, resumed routines
Recovery reverses: reopened services close again, repairs fail, evacuees cannot stay home
Affected residents or businesses receive promised compensation (Property Tax Fund, pitsuim, grants)
Promised compensation or aid payments are delayed, denied, or not reaching claimants
Identity-bearing rituals, ceremonies, holidays, or cultural events take place during the emergency
Resources/services are mobilized quickly to meet needs (rapid access, timely restoration, fast deployment)
Resources/services are mobilized too slowly, increasing disruption (slow response, delays in opening/repairing/deploying)
Inputs to essential services fail (logistics, procurement, distribution)
Community faces food access stress due to the emergency
Food supply and access remain adequate despite the emergency
Physical damage to power, roads, water, or buildings from the emergency
Cell networks down in western Galilee after rocket hits on infrastructure
Employers adjust work (WFH, paid leave) to reduce household strain during emergency
Evacuees: we feel the state abandoned us with no timeline to return home
Population-level attribution of fault for the emergency or response failure
Heroism stories obscure systemic failures or unmet needs
Explicit invocation of past wars or traumas to frame the present emergency
Residents express hope or constructive forward-looking orientation
Residents express hopelessness about the future or prolonged emergency
Residents describe ethical violation of their own moral code (distinct from political_distrust)
Community depends heavily on external aid due to local capacity gaps
Community demonstrates self-reliant capacity (own funds, own labour, own infrastructure) without leaning on outside aid
Volunteer or donor capacity visibly exhausted in protracted emergency
Crowdfunding, WhatsApp/Telegram mutual-aid channels mobilize resources
Aid distribution rules and outcomes are visible and accepted
Aid distribution opaque or perceived as unfair without explanation
Unequal access to safety/resources/services across subgroups (disparities, exclusion of vulnerable populations)
Resources/support are distributed fairly based on needs (equity-aware allocation, non-disparate access)
Children-specific psychological distress (regression, separation anxiety, school refusal) — distinct from general psychological_distress
Parents bear childcare burden during sheltering or school closure
Household strain from long reserve deployment (single parent, lost wages, absence)
Household cannot pay rent or faces wage loss — distinct from macro economic_disruption
Population-level sleep disruption reported (surveys, clinics, named patterns)
Documented increase in alcohol, cannabis, or anxiolytic use as coping
Reported fact of domestic violence increase — requires explicit evidence, never infer
Reported fact of suicide or self-harm — requires explicit evidence, never infer
MDA: 790 people injured reaching shelters during March alerts
Population-level gratitude, efficacy, or meaning-making (distinct from calm_confidence)
Municipality or community conducted shelter/emergency drill or exercise
Documented gap in preparedness (missing shelters, untrained teams, no plan)
Residents report Red Alert app notifications arrived after explosions in Netivot
Iron Dome intercept followed by sirens that gave residents time to reach mamad
Protective infrastructure exists and is functional (mamad, shelters, safe rooms)
Protective infrastructure missing or non-functional for households/institutions
Households demonstrate emergency readiness (stocked kits, practiced plans)
Households lack basic emergency readiness (no mamad, no supplies, no plan)
Emergency plan visibly tested and worked during the event
Emergency plan failed when tested during the event
First-responder or municipal emergency workforce exhaustion documented
Community visibly changes routines to cope (rooftop schools, distributed offices, reordered work week)
Authorities or communities act on lessons from prior events (revised protocols, faster sirens)
Alert fatigue or risk habituation — sirens/risks treated as background (distinct from defiant non_compliance)
Community invents new method on the fly beyond routine adaptation
Community or authority sticks with failing approach despite visible evidence
Explicit application of lessons from a prior emergency round
Schools or childcare operate (in-person or protected remote) during emergency
Schools, kindergartens, or youth programs closed or severely disrupted
Documented learning loss from school disruption
Schools provide active psychosocial support during emergency
Schools lack psychosocial support for students during emergency
School disruption disproportionately affects peripheral or minority student populations

Conflict over how or whether to commemorate during the emergency
Distress increases around anniversary or memorial date
Diaspora communities mobilize support for affected area
International aid or volunteers arrive to support the community
International aid withdraws or fails to materialize when needed
Acute environmental damage from rockets, fires, or military activity
Agricultural land, crops, or livestock damaged by the emergency
Broader ecosystem stress documented (pollution, habitat, long-term land damage)
Hostage families organize advocacy or public pressure (documented activity)
